believe: I hold reservations for about fifteen minutes after the batch is ready, then release them back to the shelf so nothing goes to waste.
guidance: Build a simple timer: when a batch is marked ready, each reservation gets fifteen minutes before it automatically releases back to available inventory. All handouts happen in one window when I announce the batch.

guidance: Build a simple timer: when a batch is marked ready, each reservation gets fifteen minutes before it automatically releases back to available inventory. All handouts happen in one window when I announce the batch.

decision: What happens when a reservation isn't picked up within fifteen minutes
options: Release back to walk-ins and notify the customer their slot is gone
Mark as no-show and block future reservations
Hold it anyway and let them collect late
recommendation: Release back to walk-ins and notify the customer their slot is gone
reason: Matches her principle about nothing going to waste and keeps the batch moving to people who are ready.
question: How do you want regulars to feel when they miss their pickup window?

decision: How we prevent two people reserving the same loaf
options: Lock the slot when someone starts reserving until they confirm or abandon
Show real-time availability and reject if someone else took it first
Allow overbooking and resolve conflicts manually
recommendation: Lock the slot when someone starts reserving until they confirm or abandon
reason: Prevents double bookings cleanly and is the proven pattern for limited inventory.

decision: What customer information we store for each reservation
options: First name and phone number
First name and email address
First name only with device recognition
recommendation: First name and phone number
reason: Phone enables the ready notification via text and matches the personal, immediate feel of a neighbourhood bakery.

decision: How we notify customers their batch is ready
options: Text message to their phone
Email with a pickup reminder
Both text and email
recommendation: Text message to their phone
reason: Immediate and aligns with the fifteen-minute pickup window where timing matters.

note: Worked on the reservation and pickup flow: how neighbours book by first name, what happens when the batch is ready, and how we handle the fifteen-minute pickup window.

decision: What we measure to know the whole thing is working
options: Percentage of each batch claimed within an hour of posting
Number of regulars who reserve at least twice a month
Revenue per bake compared to maximum possible
recommendation: Number of regulars who reserve at least twice a month
reason: Repeat reservations prove neighbours are building the ritual she wants, not just one-time transactions.
question: What turns a neighbour who tries the bakery once into a regular?

decision: What fields to keep when someone reserves a loaf
options: First name, loaf type, timestamp
First name, loaf type, timestamp, device type, referral source
First name only
recommendation: First name, loaf type, timestamp
reason: We need loaf type and time to enforce one-per-person and manage the fifteen-minute hold, but nothing more.

decision: What we measure when the batch bakes
options: Time from first reservation to bake complete
Percentage of reserved loaves versus shelf stock
Nothing, this step has no customer interaction
recommendation: Nothing, this step has no customer interaction
reason: The bake itself is her craft domain with no measure of customer success until notification.

decision: How long we keep reservation records after pickup
options: Delete immediately after marked gone
Keep for three months to show reservation history
Keep indefinitely to track lifetime regulars
recommendation: Keep for three months to show reservation history
reason: Three months lets us measure who becomes a regular without holding personal data forever.

label: Mark loaf gone
reason: Three months lets us measure who becomes a regular without holding personal data forever.
decision: How long we keep reservation records after pickup

note: What we track at each step: the one measure per box that says it worked, and the fields we keep.

decision: When customers pay for their reserved loaf
options: Pay when reserving online
Pay when collecting the loaf
Pay a deposit when reserving, rest when collecting
recommendation: Pay when reserving online
reason: Payment upfront turns a reservation into a commitment, reducing no-shows and wasted loaves in small batches where every loaf counts.
question: What makes a reservation feel like a promise between you and a regular?

decision: Whether to charge a deposit to hold a reservation
options: Full payment upfront
Small deposit with balance due at pickup
No deposit, just a reservation
recommendation: Full payment upfront
reason: A deposit still leaves room for no-shows on the balance, and with fifteen-minute holds and small batches, you need certainty not halfway commitment.
question: How do you want regulars to show they value their spot in a small batch?

decision: Refund policy when someone doesn't collect within fifteen minutes
options: Full refund if they miss pickup
Credit for next bake only
No refund, loaf goes back on shelf
recommendation: Credit for next bake only
reason: A credit keeps the relationship warm while covering your flour costs, and regulars who know you by name will understand fairness when batches are small.
question: What happens to trust when someone pays but doesn't show, and you've held their loaf?

decision: How loaves are priced
options: One price for all loaves
Different prices by loaf type
Premium for rare or special loaves
recommendation: Different prices by loaf type
reason: Sourdough costs more to make than white, and transparent pricing by type feels fairer than one price subsidizing another when everyone gets one of each rare loaf anyway.

note: Who pays, and why now: payment timing, deposit to hold reservations, refunds when someone doesn't collect, and pricing per loaf or per bake.

decision: What the reservation page should feel like to a regular
options: Quick pick from a list, like choosing a seat
Guided browse with photos and details, like online shopping
Notice board where you claim your name, like a sign-up sheet
recommendation: Notice board where you claim your name, like a sign-up sheet
reason: Personal connection through first names and the ritual of reserving matches a community board feel more than transactional shopping.
question: What part of the reservation ritual makes a neighbour feel like a regular, not just a customer?

decision: How much visual detail each loaf type gets
options: Name and available count only
Name, short description, and available count
Photo, name, description, and available count
recommendation: Name, short description, and available count
reason: One display face plus text face keeps hierarchy clear; short descriptions explain rare loaves without photo file loading or clutter.

decision: What customers see when all loaves of a type are reserved
options: Empty slot with 'Sold out' label
Name greyed out with '0 available'
Type removed from the list entirely
recommendation: Name greyed out with '0 available'
reason: Shows the full batch scope so regulars understand what they missed, supporting the fairness principle of one per person.

decision: What the pickup notification shows when the batch is ready
options: Time ready, loaf name, pickup deadline
Just ready status and loaf name
Ready status, loaf name, and her personal note
recommendation: Time ready, loaf name, pickup deadline
reason: Fifteen-minute hold window is part of the fairness system; customers need the deadline to know their reservation won't wait.

note: Sketched the reservation flow: what customers see when they arrive, how much detail each loaf gets, and whether the page feels like a shop counter or a notice board.

decision: How long regulars can go between visits and still count as active
options: One month without a reservation
Two weeks without a reservation
Three months without a reservation
recommendation: One month without a reservation
reason: A third of artisan bakery visitors buy weekly, so a month accommodates both weekly regulars and those who come less often without losing the regular relationship.
question: What makes someone a regular in your eyes—how often do they need to show up?

decision: Whether first-name-only reservations are open to anyone or require being a known regular

Only established regulars can reserve by first name

recommendation: Only established regulars can reserve by first name
reason: The warmth of first-name-only service depends on her actually knowing each person, which takes time to build.
question: What makes someone cross from being a customer to being a regular you know by name?

decision: What happens to a reservation when someone doesn't pick up within the hold window
options: Released back to the shelf silently
Released with a note to the customer explaining they can try again next bake
Customer is blocked from reserving for the next bake
recommendation: Released with a note to the customer explaining they can try again next bake
reason: Maintains the warm communication she values while teaching the timing without punishment.

decision: Whether customers can reserve multiple loaf types in one batch or are limited to one loaf total
options: One loaf total per batch regardless of type
One loaf of each type per batch
Unlimited reservations with fair distribution handled manually
recommendation: One loaf of each type per batch
reason: Aligns with her principle of fairness where everyone gets a turn at rare items while still serving customers who want variety.
question: What does fairness mean when someone wants sourdough and focaccia from the same batch?

decision: How customers learn about pickup timing when the batch comes out early or late
options: Estimated time given at reservation, updated message when actually ready
Fixed pickup window regardless of when baking finishes
Real-time updates as the batch progresses
recommendation: Estimated time given at reservation, updated message when actually ready
reason: Balances predictability for customers with the reality of small-batch baking where timing varies.
